semantics.note: The proposition keeps both antecedents (bubble bursts; Anthropic and OpenAI stop training) and his firm 'won't'. 'No justification' is evaluative, which the contract notes.

contract.note: Counting existing or third-party models as teachers is an interpretation the speaker did not supply. He may mean only future frontier teachers. The contract flags this. It does not matter yet because the antecedents have not occurred.

evidence.note: OpenAI disclosure of an 11-day safety pause, with training resumed Oct 1, 2026. This is not the post-bubble cessation the claim describes, so the antecedent is not met.
DeepSeek-R1 distillation from Jan 2025, before the forecast and before any antecedent. It shows other teachers exist but cannot test the post-condition outcome.

reviews.rationale: This conditional forecast has no deadline. Neither antecedent is verified: there is no bubble collapse and no lasting stop to training by Anthropic and OpenAI, and the OpenAI pause was temporary. Evidence from before the condition is context only. It cannot be scored yet.

semantics.note: The 'stop growing' part comes from the next sentence, a fair reading. Excluding Oracle is a scope limit, not really an antecedent, but it is kept. The four-year phrase may describe the window of analyst expectations rather than a deadline.

contract.note: Reading the claim as Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet cloud growth, with Oracle excluded, is a fair reading. The deadline and the meaning of 'cease to be' are interpretations, but they do not decide the result now.

evidence.note: Anthropic's S-1 announcement (Oct 26, 2026) shows it is still operating, so the antecedent is not met. This concerns the condition, not the outcome, so it is context rather than contradiction.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent, that both OpenAI and Anthropic cease to exist, has not occurred; Anthropic filed for an IPO. The contract horizon runs to 2030-08-25, which is after the evaluation date. A conditional whose antecedent has not happened is not scored.

semantics.note: In context, 'as a result' points to billing by tokens burned. The proposition states an incentive claim about both named labs and does not overstate it as intent.

contract.note: Testing the overall commercial incentive, net of serving costs, is a reasonable reading. Whether 'inefficient' means avoidable tokens at equal quality is an interpretation the contract supplies and flags.

evidence.note: Theoretical paper on an incentive to misreport tokenization, tested on open models. It is a different mechanism and does not cover the named providers' design economics.
Anthropic disclosure quoting a customer on token efficiency. It is a company statement, not an independent measure of incentives.
OpenAI describes engineering to reduce repeated work. Company disclosure; it does not measure incentives.
OpenAI reports efficiency gains and lower prices. Company disclosure with no data on marginal profit from extra tokens.

reviews.rationale: No item shows whether avoidable tokens raise or lower expected returns for either provider. The paper covers a related but different mechanism, and the efficiency claims are company self-disclosures. The packet leaves the incentive claim unsettled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: It is an explicit 'because' explanation with two parts: it doesn't know anything, and it generates probabilistically. The polemical framing of 'lies' is kept and read colloquially.

contract.note: An operational meaning of 'know' is the only testable reading. Not requiring intent behind 'lies' is generous to the speaker. The result does depend on this reading of 'know', which the contract flags.

evidence.note: Kalai et al. 2025: hallucinations arise from statistical pressures when facts cannot be told apart from falsehoods. Supports the probabilistic-generation mechanism.
Zhang et al. 2023: ChatGPT and GPT-4 recognized 67% and 87% of their own false claims. This cuts against an absolute 'doesn't know anything' explanation.

reviews.rationale: The probabilistic-generation part holds: e1 links statistical pressures to false outputs. The absolute 'doesn't know anything' part is contradicted, because e2 shows models can often recognize false claims they made, so they hold some accessible factual information. The full causal explanation is therefore only partly supported.
